title: From Confederation to Constitution
learningObjectives: Order key events from committee appointment in 1776 through adoption, ratification, operation, and replacement
Explain why ratification was delayed and why the central government proved ineffective
Connect weaknesses under the Articles to the decision to redesign the government in 1787

evidence.quote: One of the committees was tasked with determining what form the confederation of the colonies should take.
After considerable debate and revision, the Second Continental Congress adopted the Articles of Confederation on November 15, 1777.

explanations.text: A committee with one representative from each colony drafted the plan, and Congress adopted the Articles after debate and revision.

evidence.quote: Ratification by all 13 states was necessary to set the Confederation into motion.
Because of disputes over representation, voting, and the western lands claimed by some states, ratification was delayed.

explanations.text: Because all 13 states had to agree, disputes over representation, voting, and western lands delayed the start of government.

evidence.quote: With the states retaining considerable power, the central government had insufficient power to regulate commerce.
In May of 1787, the Constitutional Convention assembled in Philadelphia to revise the Articles of Confederation.

explanations.text: The central government could not tax or regulate commerce, so delegates met in 1787 to revise the Articles and redesign the government.

evidence.quote: After the Lee Resolution proposed independence for the American colonies, the Second Continental Congress appointed three committees on June 11, 1776.
One of the committees was tasked with determining what form the confederation of the colonies should take.
The Articles of Confederation were adopted by the Continental Congress on November 15, 1777.
This document served as the United States' first constitution.
When Maryland ratified it on March 1, 1781, the Congress of the Confederation came into being.
Ratification by all 13 states was necessary to set the Confederation into motion.
In May of 1787, the Constitutional Convention assembled in Philadelphia to revise the Articles of Confederation.
They shuttered the windows of the State House (Independence Hall) and swore secrecy so they could speak freely.
It was in force from March 1, 1781, until 1789 when the present-day Constitution went into effect.
After three hot, summer months of highly charged debate, the new Constitution was signed, which remains in effect today.
